title: Grid Paths & Pascal's Triangle
coreInsight: Path counts can be built recursively from predecessor states, and unrestricted shortest paths correspond to choosing which step positions have each direction.
targetLearnerRealization: Path counts can be built recursively from predecessor states, and unrestricted shortest paths are equivalent to choosing which step positions have one direction.
learningObjectives: Build a grid-path count by adding the counts at all possible predecessor points.
Explain why unrestricted shortest paths are counted by choosing the positions of one step direction.
Recognize when a boundary or obstacle invalidates a direct combination count and use recursive counting instead.

continuity.openingCallback: C7 ended by asking whether choosing the positions of the rightward steps could determine an entire shortest path.
closingSeeds: A route through a required checkpoint can be split into an incoming path and an outgoing path.
The value at a state can be assembled from the values at every state that can immediately precede it.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Counting grid points is the same as counting paths.
A combination formula still works unchanged when obstacles alter the path structure.
Recursive and choose-based solutions count different things.
Every path problem requires explicitly listing routes.

beats.purpose: Reactivate C7's closing idea just long enough to establish that a shortest path is determined by the positions of one direction.
beats.expectedRealization: Once the U positions are chosen, every other position must contain R, so the complete path is fixed.
beats.transitionIn: C7 ended with a shortest path containing three R steps and two U steps. Bring that question back, but focus on what information actually determines the route.
beats.transitionOut: Choosing positions counts whole paths without drawing them one at a time—but first we will discover a second count directly on the grid.
beats.prompt: For a shortest path with three R steps and two U steps, which information alone determines the entire five-step path?

options.text: The two step positions occupied by U
The total number of grid points in the rectangle
Only whether the first step is R or U

feedback.u-positions: Yes. Every unchosen position is then forced to be R.
feedback.grid-points: Grid points are locations, not complete routes through them.
feedback.first-step: The first step leaves four step positions undecided.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—the chosen U positions encode the whole route.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ask whether your information fixes all five step positions, not just part of the route.

visual.ariaLabel: Five step positions with up steps in positions two and five and right steps in the other positions

steps.body: After positions 2 and 5 are chosen for U, positions 1, 3, and 4 must be R. The choice produces exactly one path: RURRU.

resolution.takeaway: A shortest path can be encoded by choosing the positions of either step direction.

beats.purpose: Let the learner attempt a complete count on the smallest grid that has enough routes to make ad hoc listing fragile.
beats.expectedRealization: A 2-right, 2-up grid has six paths, not nine paths from its nine grid points.
beats.transitionIn: Now hide the step-position shortcut for a moment and count from the grid itself.
beats.transitionOut: The six routes are correct; the useful question is how the grid can produce that total without a route list.
beats.whyNow: A 2-by-2 move grid is small enough to verify but large enough to contrast paths with grid points and motivate a recursive count.
beats.entryBridge: A shortest route must use exactly two R steps and two U steps. Count complete routes, not visited points.
beats.exitBridge: Six is the number of full move sequences; nine is only the number of lattice points in the picture.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The fixed step positions from the opening callback, now viewed as movement on a grid.
learnerPrompts: What must the final move be for a path entering the destination from the left?
What must the final move be for a path entering from below?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Separate paths by their final move: every path arrives from exactly one of two predecessor points.

visual.ariaLabel: Three by three lattice of path counts with rows 1 1 1, 1 2 3, and 1 3 6 from start to destination

steps.title: Seed the start
steps.body: There is one way to be at the starting point before moving.

steps.title: Fill the edges
steps.body: Along either outer edge, every point has only one predecessor, so its count stays 1.

steps.title: Fill the interior
steps.body: Every interior point receives all paths from its left predecessor and all paths from its lower predecessor.

resolution.takeaway: The grid's point-counts build the number of paths; they are not themselves the paths being counted.

beats.purpose: Have the learner justify addition from a disjoint final-step split before naming the recurrence.
beats.expectedRealization: Paths arriving from different immediate predecessors form complete, non-overlapping cases, so their counts add.
beats.transitionIn: Look inside the same count grid. One point has 2 ways arriving from its left and 1 way arriving from below.
beats.transitionOut: The addition is justified because the final step places every route in one and only one predecessor case.
beats.prompt: Why should the number written at that point be 2 + 1 rather than 2 × 1?

options.text: A path arrives from the left or from below, and cannot do both on its final step.
Every left-arriving path must be paired with every below-arriving path.
The two predecessor points and the new point make three points.

feedback.final-step-cases: Exactly. The cases cover every path and do not overlap.
feedback.two-stages: A single path has one final predecessor; it does not combine two different paths.
feedback.count-points: The label counts routes into the point, not points in the diagram.

beats.incorrectFeedback: Classify each complete route by the location of its penultimate point.

visual.ariaLabel: Two non-overlapping predecessor cases with two paths and one path combining to three

steps.title: Coverage
steps.body: Every route into the point has a final R step from the left or a final U step from below.

steps.title: Non-overlap
steps.body: No route has both final steps, so no route belongs to both cases.

steps.title: Add the cases
steps.body: The two paths in the first case and the one path in the second case give three paths total.

resolution.takeaway: Ways to a state equal the sum of the ways to every possible immediate predecessor.

beats.purpose: Reconnect the grid's recursively obtained six paths to C7's choice-without-order interpretation.
beats.expectedRealization: Choosing the two U positions among four step positions counts the same six routes as the grid recurrence.
beats.transitionIn: The grid produced 6 by predecessor addition. Restore the step-position view from the opening and count the same routes again.
beats.transitionOut: Two calculations agree because each one labels the same set of complete paths in a different way.
beats.prompt: A shortest path on the tiny grid has two R steps and two U steps. How many choices are there for the two positions occupied by U?

response.feedback: Choose 2 of the 4 step positions; the remaining positions are automatically R.

beats.incorrectFeedback: Number the four step positions and choose an unordered pair for the U steps.

visual.ariaLabel: The six unordered pairs of positions chosen for two up steps among four total steps

steps.body: Each pair of U positions produces one route, and every route has exactly one such pair.
The recursive count and the choose count both count all shortest 2R-2U paths exactly once.

resolution.takeaway: Pascal-style addition and combinations are two views of the same unrestricted path set.

beats.purpose: Make the Pascal connection inspectable after the learner has independently obtained the central six by recurrence and by choosing positions.
beats.expectedRealization: The central 6 sits in a triangular array built by the same add-the-two-predecessors rule.
beats.transitionIn: Arrange the step-position counts by total number of steps. The six from the tiny grid lands in a familiar additive pattern.
beats.transitionOut: The pattern now has a name, but its meaning came first: each entry counts paths with a fixed inventory of the two step directions.

visual.ariaLabel: First five rows of Pascal's Triangle ending with one four six four one

beats.caption: Every interior number is the sum of the two numbers above it; the central 6 counts the 2R-2U paths.

beats.purpose: Name the recurrence and Pascal connection only after both representations have been constructed.
beats.expectedRealization: Pascal's Triangle records the same predecessor addition satisfied by combination counts.
beats.transitionIn: You discovered one count by adding predecessors and then recovered it by choosing step positions.
beats.transitionOut: On an unrestricted grid either view is available; a board edge will now test whether the shortcut still describes every allowed path.
beats.name: Grid-path recurrence and Pascal's Triangle
beats.conciseDefinition: Write 1 at the start. At each reachable point, add the counts at every point that can immediately precede it. On an unrestricted right-up grid, these are the same additions that build Pascal's Triangle.
beats.formalization: ways(r,u) = ways(r−1,u) + ways(r,u−1), with ways(r,0)=ways(0,u)=1; therefore ways(r,u)=C(r+u,u)=C(r+u,r).
beats.memoryHook: Add predecessors on the grid; choose direction positions in the step string.

beats.purpose: Apply the recurrence to the approved authentic checkerboard problem and confront the false unrestricted-combination distractor created by the board edge.
beats.expectedRealization: The board count is 28; C(7,3)=35 counts seven extra routes that leave the board, so unrestricted choose counting cannot be used unchanged.
beats.transitionIn: The tiny grid had no forbidden move. This checkerboard has sides, so first decide whether the same two views still count exactly the same allowed routes.
beats.transitionOut: Predecessor addition automatically respects the edge; a combination shortcut is safe only after its step strings are checked against every restriction.
beats.whyNow: The mapped checkerboard extends the learner's tiny count grid while making the unrestricted combination value 35 a deliberate distractor that exposes boundary restrictions.
beats.entryBridge: Seed P with 1 and let each reachable white square inherit the sum of the reachable squares diagonally below it.
beats.exitBridge: The waterfall reaches Q with 28; the unrestricted 35 includes seven step strings that cross the right edge.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Grid cells labeled by the number of ways to reach them from predecessor cells.
learnerPrompts: From P, which two white squares can the marker reach in one step?
For the highlighted interior square, why do the two counts diagonally below add?
Which two predecessor squares feed Q, and what total reaches it?
Why does C(7,3)=35 count paths that the actual board forbids?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—28 legal seven-step paths reach Q.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep your attempt. Build counts upward from P; do not assume every left-right step string stays on the board.

steps.title: Propagate legal path counts
steps.body: Start with 1 at P. Each reachable white square receives the sum of its reachable diagonal predecessors; missing predecessors beyond an edge contribute 0.

steps.title: Finish at Q
steps.body: The lower rows build to predecessor counts 19 and 9 beneath Q.

steps.title: Another way: audit the unrestricted shortcut
steps.body: Without board edges, choosing which 3 of the 7 steps go left would give 35 step strings. Seven cross the right edge, so they are not legal board paths.

resolution.takeaway: Recursive counts enforce local restrictions automatically; a combination count needs a correction when some step strings leave the allowed region.

beats.purpose: Give near independent practice translating an unrestricted shortest route into a choice of step positions.
beats.expectedRealization: Three right and two up steps can be placed in C(5,2)=10 orders.
beats.transitionIn: After the edge complication, return once to a clean unrestricted rectangle and choose the shortest representation.
beats.transitionOut: On an unrestricted grid, the choose count compresses the same additions the count grid would perform.
beats.whyNow: This near item checks that the learner can independently select and execute the combination representation after seeing its equivalence to recursion.
beats.entryBridge: Determine the required numbers of R and U steps before choosing positions.
beats.exitBridge: Choosing the two U positions among five fixes all three R positions.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A shortest path encoded as selected step positions.
learnerPrompts: How many total steps are forced?
Which direction's positions will you choose?
beats.incorrectFeedback: A shortest route has five step positions. Choose the two occupied by U.

groups.label: Five step positions
groups.calculation: choose 2 for U; the other 3 are R

visual.ariaLabel: Five path-step slots with two selected for up steps

steps.title: Fix the move inventory
steps.body: Every shortest route uses exactly 3 R steps and 2 U steps.

steps.title: Choose positions
steps.body: Choose the 2 U positions; every remaining slot must contain R.

resolution.takeaway: For unrestricted shortest paths, choose the positions of one required direction.

beats.purpose: Test whether the learner abandons an unchanged combination formula when one interior point is forbidden and uses predecessor counts or a valid correction.
beats.expectedRealization: Four of the ten shortest paths avoid the closed point; six pass through it and must be excluded.
beats.transitionIn: Now place one restriction inside a rectangle rather than on its edge. The move inventory is unchanged, but the allowed path set is not.
beats.transitionOut: The blocked point changes local predecessor flow, so the unrestricted total 10 is only a starting point, not the answer.
beats.whyNow: This mixed item directly diagnoses whether the learner checks restrictions before applying a combination formula unchanged.
beats.entryBridge: Give the closed point count 0, then propagate counts to the destination—or count and remove routes through it.
beats.exitBridge: Both legal methods preserve exactly the four paths that never enter the closed point.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A grid of predecessor counts, with a forbidden state contributing zero.
learnerPrompts: What count should be written at a closed point?
How does that zero affect later points?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—4 shortest paths avoid the closed intersection.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The unrestricted total is 10, but routes through the closed point are illegal. Refill the grid with 0 there.

visual.ariaLabel: Path count grid with a closed interior point labeled zero and destination count four

steps.title: Block the state
steps.body: No legal route may stand at the closed point, so write 0 there instead of adding its predecessors.

steps.title: Continue the recurrence
steps.body: Every later point still adds the legal counts from its left and lower predecessors, ending at 4.

steps.title: Connection
steps.body: There are 10 unrestricted paths. Exactly 2 paths reach the closed point and 3 paths continue from it, so 2 × 3 = 6 are forbidden.

resolution.takeaway: A restriction changes the set of paths; encode it in the recurrence or correct the unrestricted count with a justified case count.

beats.purpose: Provide challenge evidence that the learner can propagate predecessor counts through multiple restrictions without explicit route listing.
beats.expectedRealization: A count grid handles two closed points locally and produces 19 legal shortest paths.
beats.transitionIn: One final route count removes the convenient one-obstacle correction. Let the local rule carry the bookkeeping.
beats.transitionOut: Even with several restrictions, each state still asks the same small question: which legal predecessors can feed me?
beats.whyNow: The challenge rewards recursive organization: two blocked points create overlapping forbidden-route families that are awkward to subtract directly.
beats.entryBridge: Write 0 at each closed intersection and fill all other points from left and below.
beats.exitBridge: The destination count 19 already excludes every route touching either closed point, with no duplicate subtraction to manage.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The same predecessor-count grid, now with two forbidden states.
learnerPrompts: Where must the two zeros be placed before filling?
Why does each later count already exclude every illegal partial route?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—19 shortest paths avoid both closed intersections.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Fill the 5-by-5 point grid in order, forcing each closed point to 0 before its count can flow forward.

visual.ariaLabel: Five by five predecessor count grid with closed points at one right two up and three right two up, ending at nineteen

steps.title: Seed restrictions
steps.body: Place 0 at both closed points. Every other boundary and interior count follows the same predecessor rule.

steps.title: Propagate only legal partial paths
steps.body: Once an illegal partial path is stopped at a zero, it never contributes to a later point.

steps.title: Read the destination
steps.body: The upper-right point receives 10 paths from the left and 9 from below.

resolution.takeaway: Recursive counting turns global path restrictions into local zeroes and additions.

beats.purpose: Consolidate the complete decision process before opening a forward-looking question.
beats.expectedRealization: The learner can distinguish states from paths, justify predecessor addition, connect it to combinations, and audit restrictions.
beats.transitionIn: Across the tiny grid, checkerboard, and closed intersections, the pictures changed but the counting decisions stayed stable.
beats.transitionOut: The method is now larger than grids: it builds a count whenever outcomes arrive from known predecessor states.
beats.prompt: Which statements belong in a reliable grid-path toolkit? Select all four.

options.text: A number at a grid point counts paths reaching that state; it is not a count of grid points.
Add predecessor counts when final-step cases cover all paths without overlap.
For unrestricted shortest paths, choose the positions of one direction.
Before using a combination unchanged, check that every encoded step string obeys the boundaries and obstacles.
Explicitly listing every route is required before any formula can be trusted.

response.feedback: Check what the point labels mean, why addition is legal, when choose notation matches paths, and what restrictions can break that match.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—that toolkit connects the recursive and choose views without ignoring restrictions.
beats.incorrectFeedback: One option confuses a verification method with a requirement; the other four describe the actual structure.

groups.label: Compress
choices: choose direction positions on an unrestricted shortest path

visual.ariaLabel: Three-stage grid path toolkit: build by predecessors, compress with combinations, and audit restrictions

steps.title: Build
steps.body: Point labels count arriving paths. Complete, non-overlapping final-step cases justify adding legal predecessor counts.

steps.title: Connect
steps.body: On an unrestricted shortest grid, choosing direction positions counts the same paths as the recurrence.

steps.title: Restrict
steps.body: Edges and obstacles may invalidate some step strings, while recursive counts can stop them locally.

resolution.takeaway: Count locally by predecessors, recognize the equivalent choose count when unrestricted, and audit every restriction before using the shortcut.

beats.purpose: Create a forward hook from grid points to the broader idea of assembling state counts from predecessors, after consolidation is complete.
beats.expectedRealization: The recursive idea can apply whenever a process has states and allowed predecessor transitions, even without a geometric grid.
beats.transitionIn: The grid made predecessor states visible. The same logic does not actually require squares or compass directions.
beats.prompt: Suppose a process reaches each state from several earlier states, with different transitions allowed. What information would you need in order to build the number of ways to reach every state?
beats.takeaway: A path-count table is an example of a wider strategy: define states, identify legal predecessors, seed the start, and propagate counts.

notes: Draft technique lesson authored with the repo-local mathinking-lesson Skill and the approved C10 mapping.
The opening briefly reactivates C7's step-position encoding before advancing to predecessor-state counting.
Completed count grids and step-position organizations appear only in post-response resolutions.
The approved 2020 AMC 8 Problem 21 is the sole bank problem and uses its controlled four-step checker-path animation after submission.
The checkerboard's recursive solution is primary; the free-board combination correction appears afterward as a useful alternate view.
Existing choice-grid and slot-filler primitives cover all static visuals; no renderer infrastructure was changed.
After lesson-used items are excluded, the generated pool still supports the declared two-near, two-mixed, one-challenge fresh practice session.
